title: Sugihara Writes Visas Day and Night
text:
In the summer of 1940 Chiune Sugihara was the Japanese vice consul in Kaunas, Lithuania. The Soviet Union was occupying the country, and Jewish refugees from Poland and Lithuania were desperate to escape before the Nazis or the Soviets closed every door. Hundreds gathered outside the Japanese consulate asking for transit visas through Japan. Many held papers for the Dutch colony of Curacao, provided by the Dutch consul Jan Zwartendijk.

Sugihara cabled Tokyo three times for permission to issue the visas. Each time he was told not to give them to people without proper funds and final destinations. After discussing it with his wife Yukiko, he decided to disobey. For weeks, from late July to the end of August, he wrote visas by hand for many hours a day, often for whole families on a single visa. When the consulate was closed and he had to leave, he kept writing and signing papers until his train pulled out.

Thousands of refugees crossed the Soviet Union to Vladivostok, sailed to Japan and later reached Shanghai, the Americas and elsewhere. After the war Sugihara left the foreign service. In 1985 Yad Vashem recognized him as Righteous Among the Nations.
lesson: Rules exist to serve people, not to excuse us from helping them. One person's choice to act, at real personal cost, can save more lives than they will ever know.
source: Yad Vashem, Righteous Among the Nations file on Chiune Sugihara; Hillel Levine, In Search of Sugihara (1996)
caveat: Estimates of the number saved vary widely, usually given as about 2,000 visas and up to 6,000 people, and the circumstances of his leaving the foreign ministry are debated.
